title: Fibre and construction identification
audience: Carpet and upholstery cleaners who need to identify the fibre and construction before any treatment.
referencesAtStart: No legal or regulatory claims are made in this lesson. No official source was fetched for this lesson.
learningOutcomes: Identify common carpet and upholstery fibres by look, feel and the care label.
Recognise the construction, such as loop pile, cut pile or woven backing, and its effect on cleaning.
Treat an unidentified fibre as sensitive until it is tested.

instruction.heading: Why the fibre comes first
instruction.body: The fibre decides how an item responds to water, heat, brushing and product, so it has to be identified before anything else is chosen. The broad groups matter most. Protein fibres, such as wool, are usually treated with more care than cellulose fibres, such as cotton and linen, and synthetic fibres, such as nylon, polyester and polypropylene. General practice is that protein fibres are more easily damaged by heat and strongly alkaline products, and that some synthetics tolerate water better but can be marked by some solvents. These are general cleaning points. The colour of an item tells you very little about its fibre.

instruction.heading: Looking at and feeling the fibre
instruction.body: Work in good light and use a magnifier. Look at the sheen, the depth of the colour, the twist of the yarn, and whether the fibres are short and crimped or long and straight. Feel the surface and the pile. Natural fibres often feel different from synthetics, but that is a tendency, not an identification, and two fibres can feel alike. Where a loose fibre can be taken from an inconspicuous spot without damage, look at it closely. Do not use an open flame or a burn test on any item, on site or in the workshop, because the fire risk to the item, the premises and the operator is not acceptable and the test is not part of this course. Where the look and feel do not give a clear answer, record the fibre as unidentified.

instruction.heading: Construction: pile, backing and seams
instruction.body: Construction changes the method as much as the fibre does. A loop pile holds soil in the loops, and it can distort or fuzz when it is scrubbed hard. A cut pile shows brush marks and can crush under pressure, so the direction of the pile matters. A cut-and-loop pile combines both. A flatweave or woven construction has little pile to protect it, and water can move through into the backing and stay there. Look at the backing as well as the face. Check the seams and the edges. A seam that is already lifting, or a loose binding, is a condition to record before any water is used. Decide whether the item is a loose rug, a fixed carpet or a fabric upholstery, because the handling of a loose rug and a fixed carpet differs.

instruction.heading: The care label and the manufacturer's code
instruction.body: Where a care label exists, it gives the manufacturer's cleaning code. The code states what the manufacturer considers suitable, and it is the first source to follow. A code is not permission to use any product. A code that calls for a particular cleaning approach does not make every product on the market suitable for it. Read the label before the inspection, record it exactly as written, and compare it with the fibre and construction you have identified. Where the label and your identification disagree, treat the item as the more sensitive of the two until a test decides which one is right.

instruction.heading: The unidentified fibre and the conservative default
instruction.body: When the fibre cannot be identified with confidence, treat the item as sensitive. Choose the most conservative method available. In general practice that means the least water, the lowest heat and the mildest product that will do the job, and a test on an inconspicuous area before the main treatment. Record the item as unidentified, with the photographs and the reasons, so that the next person does not repeat the same guess. Never guess, and never choose the strongest method to save time or to satisfy the customer. A mild result that leaves some soil is acceptable if the limit is recorded and agreed; a damaged fibre is not.

instruction.heading: Recording the identification
instruction.body: Write down the fibre group, or the word unidentified, the construction, the backing, the label code exactly as written, and the reasons for the identification. Add a photograph taken with permission and record the method chosen and why. This record protects the business if the customer later asks why a method was used or refused. Keep the record with the job file rather than relying on memory, because the identification affects the inspection, the test and the scope agreed with the customer.

procedure: Note the item type (loose rug, fixed carpet or fabric upholstery) and its location on the job record.
Read the care label and the manufacturer code where one is present, and record it exactly as written.
Examine the pile, the backing and the seams in good light with a magnifier, and record the construction.
Identify the fibre group by look and feel, and record the reasons. Do not use a flame or a burn test.
Treat any unidentified fibre as sensitive, and choose the most conservative method the procedure allows.
Compare the label, the fibre and the construction, and where they conflict, use the more sensitive reading until a test decides.
Record the fibre, the construction, the label code, the method chosen and the reasons, with a photograph taken with permission.

workedExamples.situation: A wool-look rug has a woven backing, and the owner asks for a hot steam clean with a strong alkaline product to lift a dark patch.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you choose, and what do you record?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not use the hot steam or the strong alkaline product. The look suggests a protein fibre, and the woven backing can hold water for a long time. Check the label or the supplier's information if you can get it. If the fibre is still unidentified, treat the rug as sensitive, choose the most conservative low-water method, and test it on an inconspicuous edge first. Record the fibre as unidentified, the backing, the test and the decision, and tell the owner why the strong products are not used.

workedExamples.situation: (Example job) A loop-pile carpet in a small office has no care label, and the client wants a heavy scrub to lift a dark traffic line along the doorway.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not scrub hard. Use a gentler approach, test it in an inconspicuous area first, and work with the pile direction rather than against it. Record that the fibre is unidentified and that the traffic line may need a different method after the test. Explain the limit to the client before the work starts, and do not promise that the line will disappear.

workedExamples.situation: (Example job) A fabric armchair shows a lifting seam on one arm, and the cover may not be removable. The client asks for the chair to be washed down thoroughly.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Do you wet the area around the lifting seam?
workedExamples.reasoning: Record the lifting seam and the cover condition before any water is used, with a photograph taken with permission. Avoid heavy wetting near the seam, because water can work into the seam and the backing and stay there. Identify the upholstery fabric on the job record and handle its colourfastness under the upholstery lesson. Refer any seam or structural repair outside cleaning, and record that it was referred.

equipmentAndPpe: Care label and manufacturer code, recorded exactly as written where present
Magnifier and torch for inspecting the pile, backing and seams
White test cloth for later colourfastness or spot tests (see the testing lessons)
Camera or phone, used only with the owner's permission
Gloves for handling wet or treated items
Job record sheet for the identification and the method decision
No flame or burn-test equipment is used or carried

commonErrors.error: Assuming all carpet is synthetic because it looks modern.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the label, examine the fibre, and record the identification before choosing a method.

commonErrors.error: Using hot water or hot extraction on an item that is, or may be, a protein fibre.
commonErrors.prevention: Treat a suspected protein fibre as sensitive, choose a gentler method, and test first.

commonErrors.error: Flooding a woven backing or a flatweave item.
commonErrors.prevention: Limit the water, dry promptly, and check the backing before release.

commonErrors.error: Scrubbing a loop pile hard to lift a line.
commonErrors.prevention: Use a gentler, pile-aware method, test first, and record the limit.

commonErrors.error: Treating a care code as approval for a particular product.
commonErrors.prevention: Follow the code's intent, then select a product suited to the identified fibre and test it.

commonErrors.error: Wetting an item without recording a lifting seam or a loose edge first.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the seam and edge condition with photographs before any water is used.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: No licence, certificate or regulatory authority is involved in fibre identification, and this lesson does not grant one.
Product-specific dilution, dwell time and PPE come from the product label and SDS.
Open-flame and burn tests are not used. They create a fire risk in a home, an office or a workshop, and they are not part of the method in this course.

qualityStandard: The fibre group and construction are identified and recorded for each sample in the practical, or recorded as unidentified with reasons.
The care label, or the absence of a label, is recorded exactly.
An unidentified sample is treated as sensitive, with a conservative method chosen, in the case study.
No hot water or strong alkaline product is used on a suspected protein fibre without a test and a recorded decision.
documentationEvidence: Fibre and construction record with the label code exactly as written, or the note that no label is present
Photographs of the pile, backing and seams, taken with the owner's permission
Reasons for the identification, including any item recorded as unidentified
Method selection record, cross-referenced to the method selection lesson
summary: The fibre and the construction decide the method.
Read and record the care label first, and do not treat it as a product approval.
Treat unidentified or suspected protein fibres as sensitive, and test before the main treatment.
Limit the water on woven, flatweave and latex-backed items, and check the seams before any water is used.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why avoid hot water on a wool-look fibre?
options: It makes the colour brighter, which is the main reason to use it
It has no effect on protein fibres at any temperature
It can cause shrinkage or felting in some protein fibres

knowledgeChecks.question: A woven-backed rug is wet-cleaned heavily. What is the main risk?
options: Water can move into the backing and stay there
There is no risk if the rug is synthetic
It becomes far too bright and glossy in colour

knowledgeChecks.question: The fibre cannot be identified. What is correct?
options: Use the strongest method that is available on the truck for the job
Treat it as sensitive, use the most conservative method, and test first
Guess from the colour and proceed with the usual method for the job

knowledgeChecks.question: The care label and your identification disagree. What is correct?
options: Ignore the label because the look is more reliable
Use the less sensitive reading because it is faster
Treat the item as the more sensitive reading until a test decides
